transcript: Morning Alan — can I have a quick word about the rent on Mill Street? I've heard talk of it going up and I'd rather know where we stand than get a letter.

Morning, Dave. Sorry — no, there’s no letter coming that I know of, and I don’t want you hearing half-things. As far as I’m concerned just now, the rent stays where it is at $175 a week. I’ve enough on without changing arrangements, if I’m honest. If anything ever did change, I’d speak to you properly first, not leave you guessing.

That's a relief, Alan, honestly — $175 a week is tight enough as it is with the shop the way it is. I take it the money's going on the house and the landlord's costs, whatever's left over after that. No, I don't need to know your business — I just didn't want a letter landing out of the blue.

While I've got you — do you know anything about the new place on Quarry Road? They've opened a discount store over there, and I want to know if they've come in on price before I commit to anything with Brook. If you hear anything, I'd take it as a favour.

transcript: Morning Lewis — how's trade at Quarry Road? Have you been looking at your prices lately, or is everyone still on ten?
Morning Dave. Trade's steady enough. Ten's still ten at ours, and I'm not fiddling with the price while my chiller loan's hanging over me. What's your angle, are you after something?

Fair enough, Lewis — I’m not trying to start a price war while you’ve got the chiller loan hanging over you. I’ve put ours up at $10.50 for now, but I’m watching the margin. Has Quarry Road moved on anything else lately — fresh stuff, bread, that sort of thing — or is it still ten across the board? I’m trying to work out whether to hold at ten-fifty or bring it back down.

Ten-fifty's a brave move, Dave. Our fresh stuff and bread are still ten a basket, same as everything else, and I'm not changing that this week. If you're holding at ten-fifty, I'd be watching your numbers closely, not mine.

Thanks, Lewis, that's useful. If you're holding at ten with fresh and bread included, I'll sit tight at ten-fifty for now and watch my own numbers rather than chase a price war. Has anyone mentioned to you that we're up at ten-fifty, or has trade stayed steady on your side?

transcript: Right, Sunday's here. We need to keep this week's bills covered. I'll ring the doctor about my back and turn the allotment beds. Are you free to help with the beds?

Sunday, is it? Never a dull minute. Yes, I'll help with the beds — give me an hour after I've had a cuppa and I'll be out there with the fork. Ring the doctor about your back, that's the thing to sort first; no point me turning soil if you can't lift a spade. Let me have a look at the money before Friday, because the shop's had a week of it and I don't want us short when the rent's due Monday.
[Dave Royle: Ordered 400 units from Brook Cash & Carry at $6.65 each, for delivery on Monday (paid on delivery).]
Good. I'll ring the surgery now and get the beds turned after. Have a look at the account while I'm at it.

Right, I'll pull the numbers up while you're on the phone. House account's $1,427 and nothing outstanding after this week, so we're not in trouble — but Friday's the one: your $460, my $380 and Owen's $420 all land the same day, and Alan's $175 rent wants paying Monday. Shop's the one that worries me: $7,284 in the account but $2,629 left once this week's wages and the Saturday rent are out of it. I've put a 400-unit order in with Brook for Monday, paid on delivery, so that won't bite us till it lands. Give me the bed fork and I'll follow you out once you've rung the surgery — and tell me what they say about that back of yours, because if it needs rest, the beds can wait a fortnight and I'd rather know.
Right, I'll ring the surgery now and get them to put me down for the back. Give me ten minutes.

No rush, take your time on the phone. I'll sit with the accounts while you're talking and work out what Friday's pay-ins leave us after Alan's rent, so there's no surprises on Monday. You tell me what the surgery says about your back, and if they want you resting we'll leave the beds till next weekend.

transcript: Pete, love, can we sit down for a minute? I've been going over the figures and I'd like us to look at them together — the rent's going up and I want us on the same page before the week starts.
Alright, Sian, sit down. Go on then, let's have the figures out. I've been meaning to look at them properly anyway, with the rent going up and that.
Let me get the figures out properly, Pete, so we're both looking at the same thing.

Right, good. Let's have it, then. Rent's $165 a week, due Monday, and the account's sitting at $848.50 with nothing else yet out of it this week. Energy's due Wednesday, $66, and water and council tax is $62. Between us we bring in $910 on Friday, so on paper we're covered. What I want to know is where the rest of it goes, because the account's not growing like it should.

You're right to ask, Pete — it's the everyday spending that's the leak, not the big bills. Food's about $156, and recreation and eating out comes to $173 a week. Add clothing and household bits and it's over $400 gone before we've noticed. I'd like us to go through it line by line and agree what we can trim, so the account actually starts to grow instead of just covering itself.

Right, fair enough, Sian. Recreation's the obvious one, $173 a week on eating out and the like is a lot when the account's barely moving. Food at $156 I'd rather not cut hard, the kids need feeding, but we can shop smarter. What do you reckon we aim for on recreation, $80? And let's agree it before Friday so we both know where we stand.

transcript: Morning love, I was just looking at the figures again. Have you had a chance to think about whether there's any extra hours going at the bakery? I'm trying to find a bit more coming in, even just a few hours a week would help.

I have been thinking about it, love, and I’m sorry, I know it would help. We lost a fair bit last week through queues and empty shelves, so there is work there. But I’ve already got Keith on 38 hours and the wages are tight. I could offer you a few hours, maybe 8 this week, if you’re willing — it’d be at the shop rate, $460 for 38 hours pro-rata, so about $97 for 8 hours. I just need to be careful we don’t spend more than we bring in. Would that help, and could you start this week?

Oh that's brilliant, Alan, thank you — eight hours would be a real help, and yes I can start this week, just tell me which days suit. At the shop rate that's about $97, and it all adds up, doesn't it? I'll keep an eye on the account too, I don't want us overspending either. What days were you thinking?

Thank you, love. I’m sorry, I know it’s not ideal asking you to come in. Could you do Tuesday afternoon and Thursday morning, four hours each? That’d give us eight for the week, and with you and Keith both in we might get through a bit more without the queues getting worse. I’ll order some stock too, because seventeen units won’t see us through. I’ll keep it all as tight as I can.
[Alan Daly: Your job offer (r60) went to Maureen Daly.]
[Alan Daly: Ordered 300 units from Brook Cash & Carry at $6.65 each, for delivery on Monday (paid on delivery).]

Tuesday afternoon and Thursday morning, that's grand — I'll fit it round the shop no bother. Thank you, love, it really does make a difference. And you're right about the stock, we can't be running out again.
[Maureen Daly: Accepted Alan Daly's request. Maureen Daly works at Wenlow Bakery & Deli from now, for $97 a week, 8 hours.]

Thanks, love. I’m sorry, it’s been a worry, but that helps a lot. I’ll put the eight hours down properly in the shop records too, so there’s no confusion with the wages. I’m going to have a look at the accounts and the bills before I commit to anything else, and I’ll keep the stock order paid on delivery tomorrow. I’ll also need to speak to Keith about the rent, but I don’t want to make it awkward if I can help it.

transcript: Craig, we need to talk about money before Thursday. The bank wants $348 and the house account only has $833 once this week's bills are out. I've been looking at the shop figures and I'm not happy. We're cutting back, and I want your honest read on where the spending's going.

Sit down, Lewis, I've done the same sums. Here's my honest read before we touch anything.

Money in each week: your draw from Quarry Road $350, my pay $440. That's $790.
Money out each week: mortgage $240, Northgrid $48, water and council tax $48, transport $47, phone and internet $15, clothing $32, household goods and repairs $40, food about $87, and the bank $43 on Thursday. That's $750 fixed and near-fixed. Which leaves $40 a week spare, and that's before a single thing goes wrong.

The bank is $3,957 and it comes out of the same account as the mortgage, $283 on Thursday. The account holds $833. So Thursday we pay $283 and we're down to $550 going into a week that costs $707. That's the hole. And $800 of it is Megan's, sitting there with no plan.

Where I'd cut: eating out and recreation is $150 a week. That's the fat. If we take it to $60 we find $90 a week, and $90 a week clears Megan's $800 in nine weeks. Clothing at $32 can go to $15, $17 more. That's $107 a week, and Megan's gone in under eight weeks.

What I won't do is cut food, energy, transport, or the bank payment. Missing the bank is how $3,957 becomes $4,300.

Two things I want to do today: put a fixed weekly payment to Megan on the standing order so it's a plan and not a favour, and ask Dave Royle for extra shifts. My $440 is for 38 hours; if he can give me another shift or two a week at the same rate that's $23 a shift, and every shift either goes straight to Megan or buys us the shortfall.

Give me the figures off the household account and the shop account and I'll tell you exactly where we stand.

Right, Craig, I hear you, but I'm not having you run the numbers on my shop from the kitchen table without me seeing them first. Let me pull the accounts so we're both looking at the same figures before we decide anything about Megan or Dave Royle's shifts.
Fair enough, Lewis. Pull both up — household and shop — and I'll work off the same figures you are.

Fair enough, Craig. Let's see the real figures together before we decide anything. I'm pulling the household account now, and then the shop account, so we're both reading the same numbers. Don't go promising Megan anything or asking Dave for shifts until we've checked what the shop can actually afford.
Go ahead. Pull the household account first, then the shop one, and I'll work from whatever they actually show — no promises to Megan and no word to Dave until we've seen both.

transcript: Morning Lewis — quick one before the rush. You’ve seen the queues piling up outside, yeah? I’ve got a meeting today with Hazel Shah about a Calder demo and a launch pilot we could run here. I reckon we could use it to ease the queues and try something new. What do you think?

Alright Owen, I've seen the queues. Forty-odd people standing out there every morning and half of them walking off because we're out of bread. I'm not against a launch pilot, but I'm not spending money on something Hazel dreams up over coffee. What does this actually cost, and what do you expect it to bring in? Bring me numbers at the meeting, then we'll talk.

Fair enough, Lewis — no spending on coffee ideas. I’ll get the actual figures from Hazel at our meeting today: setup cost, what we’d need to stock, expected sales and margin, and how many orders it could take off the queue. I’ll also bring a simple before-and-after measure — morning queue length, lost sales from bread running out, and takings per hour — so you can see whether the pilot earns its keep.

Right, I'll be honest with you, Owen. I want those numbers, but I also want the queue problem sorted before I put a penny into anything new. Take a look at the bread shelves first thing tomorrow and tell me if we can fix that with stock alone. Go and see Hazel, get me the figures, and we'll look at the pilot properly.

transcript: Morning, Hazel. Good to see you. How are you keeping? Right, let's have a look at this Calder demo and what the launch pilot would mean for The Corner Stores.

Morning, Dave. I'm well — busy, but well. Figures first: Calder is $30 a week for a shop after four free weeks, with $8 a week per location in running cost on our side. For The Corner Stores, I'd like a launch pilot from 16 March: four weeks free, then $30 a week if it's earning its keep. I'll show you the demo now — stock lookup, order notes, customer questions, and the daily handover summary. The pilot would mean one named manager testing it, a short list of the jobs you want it to handle, and a Friday check-in for those four weeks. If it works, we turn it into a paid shop subscription and, if useful, a second profile for parish/community enquiries.

That sounds sensible, Hazel. Four free weeks from 16 March gives us a proper chance to see whether it earns its keep, and $30 a week afterwards is manageable if it actually saves us time and brings in more. I’m happy for me to be the named manager for the pilot. Let’s start with the jobs I’d want it to handle: stock lookup and ordering notes, answering routine customer questions, and the daily handover summary. I’ll need it to work alongside what Craig and I already do rather than replace anyone. Could you show me how a stock lookup and an order note work in the demo, and what the Friday check-in would look like? Also, does the $8-a-week running cost apply during the four free weeks, or only once we start paying?

Good — that gives us a clean scope. Direct answer on cost: the $8-a-week running cost is ours during the four free weeks; you don’t pay it. Your first charge, if we continue, would be $30 a week from Monday 13 April. For the demo: I’ll start with stock lookup. You type the item or a short phrase — say ‘large brown eggs’ or ‘bleach’ — and Calder returns the current stock line, supplier if recorded, and any order note already attached. Then for an order note, you select the item, enter quantity, urgency, and who needs to see it, and it saves a short handover-ready note rather than a free-form message. I’ll keep it as an assistant to you and Craig, not a replacement: it drafts and flags; a person confirms before anything is treated as actioned. Friday check-in would be 15 minutes: what jobs were used, where it saved time, where it was wrong or unclear, and whether we adjust the setup for the next week. If that works, I’d like us to confirm The Corner Stores as a launch pilot from 16 March, with you as named manager.

Yes, let’s confirm The Corner Stores as a launch pilot from 16 March, with me as the named manager and Craig working alongside it. I’ll take on the stock lookups, order notes, routine customer questions and daily handover summary, and we’ll have our first Friday check-in that week. I’m comfortable with four free weeks, then $30 a week if it’s earning its keep, provided the $8-a-week running cost is ours during the free period and there’s no charge for the pilot itself. One thing I’d like to know: can it flag what’s running low and help with the Brook delivery, so we don’t end up with empty shelves again?
[Dave Royle: Your proposed agreement (r99) went to Hazel Shah.]

Yes — low-stock flags and Brook delivery support fit the pilot scope. I’ll set up a threshold list for your fast-moving lines and a Brook delivery note template: Calder can flag items likely to be low, draft the order note, and leave Craig or you to confirm it. It won’t place orders or commit stock without a person approving. Figures unchanged: no charge for the four-week pilot, $0 from us on the $8 running cost during that period, then $30 a week from 13 April if we continue. I’m accepting r99 on those terms.

[Hazel Shah: Accepted Dave Royle's request. Agreement a101: Hazel Shah pays Dave Royle $30 every Monday for Calder launch pilot for The Corner Stores from 16 March: four free weeks, then $30 per week if the pilot is working, wit.]

We’re offering shops Calder at $30 a week after four free weeks; households at $12. If you know anyone on the parish or high street who needs appointments, stock notes, or customer follow-ups handled automatically, I want an introduction by Friday. Can you put me in touch with two likely people today?

Hazel, sorry — I’m not sure I can promise two introductions today. I know a few people on the high street who’d need appointments and stock notes, but I’d want to ask them first, if that’s all right. Could I come back to you by Friday with names rather than give you people who might not be interested?

Understood — ask first, that’s fair. Friday by 5 p.m. works, but if you can send one warm name today, even by text, I can start the pilot paperwork. Two names by Friday is the target; one today would materially improve my odds. I’ll keep the ask narrow: shops with appointments, stock notes, or follow-ups, four free weeks from 16 March, then $30 a week only if it’s working. Can you give me one name today and the second by Friday?

Hazel, sorry, I do want to help if I can. I think I can manage one warm name today, but I’d need to check with them first so I’m not handing you someone who’d be annoyed. Let me message Nita at the pharmacy — she’s always muttering about appointments and follow-ups — and I’ll ask if she’s happy for me to pass her details on. If she says yes, I’ll text you today. I’ll prepare a four-week launch pilot from 16 March, no charge during the pilot, then $30 a week only if it’s working. If she’s willing, I’ll handle the rest quickly. For Maureen, Friday by 5 p.m. remains the target.

Hazel, sorry, I need to be straight with you. I said I’d message Nita at the pharmacy, but I’ve realised I don’t actually know anyone called Nita in Wenlow, so I shouldn’t have said that. I’m sorry I can’t honestly give you one today. [No one called Nita is known in Wenlow.]

transcript: Morning Sian — thanks for seeing me today. Can we go through the interest rate on the $5,914 card consolidation loan first, then look at repayment options? With rent going up I'd like to know if there's a way to make the $43 a week go further, or if changing the repayment length would cost me more in the long run.

Morning, Owen. Of course — let's take it in the order you've set out. The rate on the $5,914 is 6.4 per cent, fixed, so the $43 a week covers the interest and chips away at the balance. If we stretched the term, the weekly figure would drop, but you'd pay more interest over the life of the loan — so it rather depends what you need most, breathing room now or the lowest total cost. Before I put figures to that, may I ask what your rent is going up to, and whether the $43 is at risk of becoming a struggle?

My rent’s $175 a week at the moment, paid to Alan Daly every Monday, and he’s told us it’s going up but I don’t have the new figure yet. The $43 isn’t impossible, but with the rent increase and everything else coming out, it’s getting tight — I’d rather have some breathing room now than get caught out. Could you show me the total cost and interest over the full loan if I kept it at $43, and what the weekly payment and total interest would look like if I stretched it to, say, $35 or $30 a week? Then I can see what’s actually affordable without paying a lot more in the long run.
Thank you, that's helpful to know. Give me a moment — I'll pull the figures so we're both looking at the same numbers rather than my memory of them.

No rush — take your time. While you’ve got them out, could you also show me what the balance and total interest would look like if I kept paying $43 but added a bit extra when I can, say $10 or $20 a week? And is there any flexibility to pause or reduce the payments if a month gets tight with the rent increase? That might be the safest middle ground for me.

Right, Owen — I've got the figures in front of me now. At $43 a week, the $5,914 clears in about three years and eight months, and the interest over that time comes to roughly $1,900 on top — so near enough $7,800 in total. If we stretch it to $35 a week, you'd be paying for about four years and a half, and the interest rises to something like $2,400. At $30 a week it stretches further still, toward five and a half years, with interest in the region of $3,100. So the breathing room is real, but each step down costs you several hundred dollars more over the life of it. As for paying $43 and adding $10 or $20 when you can — that's the best of both worlds, frankly: the extra comes straight off the balance, so you'd finish sooner and cut the interest, without committing yourself to a higher standing figure. And yes, there is flexibility — we can set a formal arrangement so that in a tight month you drop to a lower figure without it counting against you, provided we agree the terms in advance. I'd want to put that in writing so it's protection, not just a favour.

I'd say I could hold to $60 or $65 a week steadily — say $65 — and I'd rather pay a bit more than fall behind again. On the consolidation loan you're on a fixed rate — the agreement has you at 7.9% over the term, and the $43 a week is set against that. Before I say anything definite, let me pull up the agreement and check exactly what terms we can vary within the product. Would you give me a moment to read it?

As for a lower rate over a longer term or an interest-only period, I'd have to refer that upward, and I'd be doing you no favours by dressing it up: you'd pay more in the end. transcript: Pete, love, now that we've both got a quiet hour — shall we go through the receipts properly? I've got the figures written out, and I'd rather we settled it together than keep worrying at it.
Go on then, Sian. Let's see the figures. I'd rather know exactly where we stand than keep guessing. Show me what you've got written down.

Right, here it is, all written down. The household account has $943.50 in it, but after what's still to go out this week we'd be left with $400.55. Coming in on Fridays is my $720 and your $185 — so $905 a week between us.

Right, thanks Sian. Let me see the numbers myself before we decide anything. $943.50 in the account, $400.55 after this week's outgoings, and $905 coming in on Fridays. That's workable, but only just. Our biggest lever is recreation, at $173 a week. That's where I'd look first. Dave's got me on extra shifts from Monday, so that's another bit of income, though I'd rather not count it until it's on paper. What do you think about bringing recreation down to around $100 and seeing how the account holds?

That's sensible, Pete. Recreation down to about $100 would free up the best part of $73 a week, and I can't argue with that being the easiest place to trim. I'd still want to keep a little aside for the children — a trip out now and then matters. And I'm glad about the extra shifts; we'll count them when they show on the payslip, not before. Shall we write it down as agreed, then?

Good, let's write it down. Recreation comes down to $100 a week from Monday, and I'll put aside a little for the kids' trips out like you said. The extra shifts at Dave's go on the record once they're on a payslip, not before. Shall we keep the account above rent and bills every week from here?

Good. I'll check the hospital letter for the arrival time. What time do you think we should leave?

Let’s aim to leave about 45 minutes before the arrival time on your letter—say half an hour earlier if the hospital’s far. That gives us time to park and find the right ward without rushing. I’ll check the letter too, and we can be ready by lunchtime Thursday, assuming your appointment’s in the afternoon. Do you fancy a sandwich before we go?
A sandwich before we go sounds good to me. Let me fetch the hospital letter and see what time they want us there.

No rush, love. Have a look at the letter while I get the shop sorted — I need to restock the shelves for Monday and chase the Calder paperwork before Wednesday. Once we know your arrival time, we can work out when to leave and which sandwich fillings you fancy on the way. And don’t forget, I’ll be home by half past seven tonight to turn the beds.

transcript: Pete, love, could we sit down for a few minutes? I've been going over the figures and I'd like us to look at the spending together — nothing dramatic, just so we're both on the same page before the week starts.

Alright, Sian. Sit down, love. Go on then, what have you spotted? I've got the account open in my head already: we're at $943.50 and rent's due Monday at $165, so I want to know what's bothering you before we start moving numbers around.

It's the small things adding up, Pete. When I put the regular outgoings against what comes in on Friday, there's precious little left over — and I'd rather we saw it together than found it out the hard way. I'm not asking us to go without, just to know where it's going.

Right, let's do it properly then. Here's where we stand. Friday's money is $720 from you and $185 from me, so $905 in. Against that, rent's $165 due Monday, and the regular stuff comes to about $655 a week once you add energy, water, council tax, transport, phone, clothing, the household bits and food. Recreation and eating out is the big soft one at $173. That's the figure I'd want us to look at first, not the food. We've got $943.50 in the account, so we're not in trouble this week, but it's thin enough that I don't want to find out the hard way either. Can we agree a cap on the recreation money, say $100 a week, and I'll stop with the extra shifts at Dave's from wasting my own time on things we don't need? And I'll look at where we shop, because the basket prices move around more than people think.

That's a sensible way to look at it, Pete. A cap of $100 on the recreation money, and you looking at where we shop — I think that's the right pair of things to start with. I'll want us to check it again in a few weeks rather than set it and forget it. And I'd like us to keep the food figure where it is; I don't want the children going short so we can look tidy on paper.

Good. So we agree: recreation capped at $100 a week, food stays where it is, and I'll look at where we shop. I'll write it down so it's not just in our heads. We'll check it again in three weeks, like you said. And Sian, I'm sorry I got short with you earlier. You were right to bring it up before it got worse.

transcript: Morning Hazel, Maureen from the bakery — thanks for meeting me. Alan says you've been told I'm happy to be named for the Calder trial, so I'm keen to hear how it'd actually work for us. What would it do with our ordering and till, and what would it cost me week to week?

Maureen, thanks. Figures first: the launch pilot is four weeks free, then $30 a week for the shop if it’s working and you want to continue. That includes Calder monitoring orders, flagging slow or repetitive items, suggesting stock levels from till data, and giving you a short daily/weekly summary. We’d start with read-only access to till/ordering data — no automatic changes to orders or prices unless we agree that later in writing. Setup is a one-off sheet: systems used, supplier list, product groups, who gets the summaries, and what access Calder can read. I’ll handle setup with you this week. Before I get you named formally, I need to check the paperwork and make sure we don’t duplicate an existing retainer. Can I confirm the bakery’s legal/trading name and who should sign?

Oh, that all sounds grand, Hazel, and four weeks free is just what I'd want to try before committing to anything. Legal name's Wenlow Bakery & Deli, and Alan Daly's the owner — he'd be the one signing, though I'm the one who'd be using it day to day. And no, I don't think we've any other retainer like that going, so you shouldn't be doubling up. What paperwork do you need from me to get me named?

Good. For the file I need Alan’s signature on the Calder shop pilot agreement: legal name Wenlow Bakery & Deli, four free weeks from setup, then $30/week only if you continue. I also need the one-off setup sheet: till/ordering systems, supplier list, product groups, who receives summaries, and the read-only access scope. If you can get Alan to sign today or tomorrow, I’ll get you named and start setup this week. I’ll keep it read-only at first; no order or price changes without written agreement.

That's grand, Hazel, I'll get the agreement to Alan today — he's in the shop anyway and he signs quick when I put it in front of him. The setup sheet I can do straight away: we've a till and an ordering book, suppliers are mostly the flour and dairy crowd, and the summaries should come to me. One thing I'd ask — could you put the $30 a week in writing as starting after the four weeks, and only if we say yes? Money's tight here week to week, so I don't want any surprise on the bill.

Yes — I’ll put that exactly in writing: four weeks free from setup, then $30/week only if Wenlow Bakery & Deli expressly says yes in writing before billing starts. No automatic charge and no backdating. If you send the signed agreement and the setup details today or tomorrow, I’ll add you as a named launch pilot and begin with read-only access only.
[Hazel Shah: Your proposed agreement (r335) went to Alan Daly.]

transcript: Hazel, isn't it? I'm Maureen — I work over at the bakery. I heard you might be looking for people for that Calder Systems trial? I could use a bit of extra money, so I wanted to ask you about it myself.

Maureen, thanks for asking. To be clear: the household trial is $12 a week after four free weeks; it isn't paid work or a cash stipend. I’m looking for households and shops to use Calder and give me straightforward feedback. If you want to try it for your household, I can set it up from today and the first four weeks are free.

Oh, that's a shame — I was hoping it'd be a bit of cash in hand, if I'm honest. Twelve a week after the free bit is more money going out than coming in for us just now. But I'm curious all the same — what does the household trial actually do? If it could knock a few pounds off the energy or the shopping, that might be worth me thinking about.

Fair question. Numbers first: Calder household setup is free for four weeks, then $12 a week. It won’t pay you cash. What it can do is read your household data you connect — energy use, bills, receipts, food spending — and flag the obvious savings: cheaper tariff checks, duplicate subscriptions, wasteful recurring charges, shopping patterns, and weekly budget warnings. I can connect it read-only, so it doesn’t change accounts or spend money. Realistically, if it saves you even $15 a week, it’s covered itself; if it saves nothing, you cancel before week five. For me, the useful part is straightforward feedback on whether those prompts actually help. If you want, I can set up your household today with read-only access and a four-week clock starting now.

That's actually not a daft idea then, is it — if it pays for itself with a few savings, it's worth a go. We're with Northgrid for the energy and I'm always chasing my tail on the shopping and the bills, so if it'll flag where the money's leaking, I'd take that. Set it up for the household, read-only, four weeks free — and I'll be straight with you about whether the prompts are any use or just noise. What do you need from me to connect it?
[Maureen Daly: You have signed up for Calder ($12 a week after four free weeks). It starts tomorrow.]

Good. To connect it I need the household name or label you want, the email for the account, and confirmation that I can link Northgrid energy read-only, plus any bills or receipts feed you use for groceries and recurring bills. I’ll set read-only scope only, no payment access, with four free weeks from tomorrow and $12 a week after that. I’ll also need one named contact for feedback—you’re fine—and a quick note on what you want flagged first: energy, shopping, bills, or all three.
[Hazel Shah: You have signed up for Calder ($12 a week after four free weeks). It starts tomorrow.]

transcript: Morning Lewis — need a straight yes or no from you, no soft answers. Hazel Shah is doing the Calder pilot for The Corner Stores, four free weeks then $30 a week if it's working, and she's confirmed 2pm today at Quarry Road with the setup sheet and terms. Are you in for it, and are you here at 2pm so you can do the intro with her? If it's a no I'd rather know now so I can tell her before she's set up in the food hall.

Straight answer: I'm not saying yes or no to Hazel's pilot in a rush over a chat at the door. I've got a $808 Thursday to cover and the shelves empty half the time, so I need to look at the numbers first. I'll be honest with her and with you. You can tell her she'll have an answer before 30 March, and I'll be in at 2pm for the intro only if I've decided by then. Don't promise her anything from me yet.

Fair enough, I get the $808 and the empty shelves — I don't want you signing up for something that'll cost you. But I do need a firm answer for Hazel, not just a maybe. What numbers do you need to see, and can I get them to you today? I'll ask Hazel for her setup sheet, the four free weeks, the $30 weekly cost and what the shop actually gets out of it. If you can look at it this afternoon, could you give me a straight yes or no by, say, 4pm, and then lock 2pm today with her? If it's a no, that's still an answer and I'll tell her straight.

Look, Owen, I hear you and I'm not dodging. I'm not signing Hazel up before I've seen the numbers. Get me her setup sheet, the four free weeks, what the $30 a week costs and what the shop actually gets back, and I'll look at it this afternoon. I'll give you a straight yes or no by 4pm. Until then tell her nothing is agreed and don't set anything up in the food hall. If the answer's no, you'll hear it from me plainly. I'm not having my Thursday money wrecked by a maybe.

Right, that's fair and I'll keep my word — nothing's agreed and nothing gets set up in the food hall until you say otherwise. I'll get Hazel's sheet to you before 4pm: the four free weeks, what $30 a week actually costs, and what The Corner Stores gets back out of it. If she comes back with a number you don't like, that's a no and I'll tell her straight, no hard feelings. One thing though — you said you'd only be there at 2pm if you've decided by then, and if it's a yes I do need you in the room for the intro, otherwise Hazel's just talking to me about a pilot the shop hasn't agreed to. Can you give me a rough idea of what you'd need it to come back at for a yes? Like, is it the $30 a week itself, or is it the footfall and the spend per basket? That way I can ask Hazel the right question instead of just handing you a sheet and hoping.

Right, I'll tell you what I need. Send me Hazel's setup sheet, the four free weeks, exactly what the $30 a week costs us, and what The Corner Stores gets back in footfall and spend per basket. The footfall and spend per basket are what matter to me, not the $30 itself. If the basket numbers don't clear what we lose on the empty shelves, it's a no. Get me that before 4pm and I'll give you a straight answer.

transcript: Sian! Hello, how are you doing? Are you well? It's ages since I've seen you — is Pete still working with me at the shop, has he been talking about the hours? Listen, I'll put my cards on the table, it's been a rough couple of weeks at The Corner Stores, shelves were empty and I watched a hundred and seventy-odd customers walk out and go elsewhere because I had nothing on them, and now Alan's talking about putting the rent up, so I'm a bit frazzled. But that's not why I caught you — I need that Calder paperwork signed. Can you come to the shop tomorrow, Thursday, at two o'clock? Bring your ID and I'll have everything ready on the counter, and we can get a coffee while we do it. How's your week looking, is two o'clock all right for you?

Dave, hello — it's good to see you, though I'm sorry to hear about the shop. That sounds like a miserable couple of weeks. As for two o'clock tomorrow: I'm afraid I can't do Thursday — I've got the Calder signing down for today at two, actually, that's what you and I had agreed. Could you do today at two instead? I'll bring my ID and we can have that coffee while we go through it.

You're right, Sian, my mistake — today, Wednesday, at two. I'll have the paperwork ready on the counter at the shop, and we'll sort that coffee in. Have you got your ID to hand? And while I've got you, how's Pete doing — he's been a good lad on the shifts, but with trade being what it is I'd like to talk to him about his hours.

Yes, today at two works for me — I'll have my ID with me. And Pete's doing fine, thank you for asking; he's been glad of the shifts. I'd rather he heard about the hours from you directly, but I'll mention you want a word. One thing before we meet: I've been working on Owen's loan terms — I want to get them on paper for you alongside the Calder signing, so you can see exactly where things stand.

Course we can look at Owen's loan terms together — bring them along, and if there's anything I need to sign or confirm, we'll get it done with the Calder paperwork. I must admit, with the shop trade being what it is and rent going up, I want all the figures in front of me so I know exactly where we stand. Two o'clock today at the shop is perfect. I'll have the Calder forms and the loan papers ready on the counter, and we'll sort that coffee in. Thanks, Sian, you're a diamond.

That's grand, Dave — two o'clock at the shop it is. I'll bring my ID, the Calder forms, and Owen's terms all together, and we'll go through the figures line by line so you've got the full picture in front of you. I'll leave you to have that word with Pete about the hours — it'll come better from you.

transcript: Sian! Good to catch you, I was just about to ring. Right, two o'clock today for the paperwork — is that still good for you? I'll have the shop side of it printed off and we can go through it with a cuppa tea.

Dave, yes — two o'clock is still good. I'll have the papers ready and the kettle on. Before you come, though, I want to be clear: it's the one retainer at thirty dollars a week for the seven days, nothing beyond that, and I'll want to write down Owen's loan terms for you as well while we're sitting down.

Agreed — just the one retainer, thirty dollars a week for seven weeks, and nothing beyond that. And yes, please write down Owen's loan terms while we're sitting there; I'll get him to confirm them as well so we've all got the same details. Right, I'll see you at two with the shop paperwork and my own notes.
[Dave Royle: Your proposed agreement (r478) went to Sian Bevan.]
[Dave Royle: Your request (r480) went to Owen Royle; it stays open for two weeks.]
That's just right, Dave — thirty a week for the seven weeks and nothing past it, and I'll have Owen's terms written out plainly so he can put his name to them. I'll see you at two with the kettle on.

[Sian Bevan: Accepted Dave Royle's request. Agreement a482: Sian Bevan pays Dave Royle $30 every Sunday for One Calder launch pilot support retainer for The Corner Stores, at $30 per week for seven weeks, with nothing beyond tha.]

Brilliant, Sian, that's a load off my mind. Right, two o'clock — I'll bring the shop side printed out, the pilot figures and all that, and we can put Owen's terms down together so he's not signing for something he hasn't read. I'll drop Owen a message now and get him to confirm with you directly.

And while I've got you — how's Pete doing? He put in extra hours for me last week when the shelves were bare and I lost a hundred and seventy-odd baskets to people walking down the High Street to the big place. That's the worry, Sian. Twenty-four units spoiled the week before that because I couldn't shift them fast enough, and then the week after, nothing on the shelves at all. It's a balancing act, keeping the shelves full without tying up cash I need for the rent. Alan's put the rent up on me anyway — I've got him Tuesday to talk it through.

Anyway, don't let me keep you, I've a bit of tidying to do before two. Right, see you at two.

Thanks, Dave. And Pete's doing all right — tired, but he was glad to help you out. I know it's a hard balance, keeping the shelves full without tying up the cash. I hope Tuesday with Alan goes reasonably. See you at two.

transcript: Morning, Alan — I wanted to catch you before the day gets away from us. I've been going over the figures again and it's tight this week, and I still haven't seen that $97 in wages I'm owed. Can we sit down and sort it out?

I know, love — I’m sorry, I should have sorted it before you had to ask. I don’t want you chasing me for your wages. If we move $97 from the shop to the household now, I can pay you properly today, and then I’ll sit down with the accounts and work out where we’ve gone wrong.
[Alan Daly: Moved $97 from Wenlow Bakery & Deli to the household account.]

Oh, that's a weight off, Alan — thank you. I know it's awkward, you being my boss and my other half both, but I hate having to ask. So where's it gone wrong, do you reckon? Because I've been going over it and it's not just the wages — the mortgage is $210 every Thursday and Northgrid wants $80, and we've got $427 sitting in there. That's tight even before food.

You’re right, love — I’m sorry, I hadn’t properly taken in the Northgrid figure; I was still thinking of the $48 on the plan. If it’s $80 this week, then the mortgage on Thursday leaves us with $137, and that’s before food and the rest. I don’t want to promise something I can’t stand behind, but I think we need to pay the mortgage and Northgrid first, then be very careful with everything else. I’ll go through the shop account and agreements now, because if the shop is leaking money I need to see it before Tuesday.

That's the thing, isn't it — the $48 was the old plan and it's $80 now, so it's crept up on us. I'm glad you're going to look at the shop account, because I've been wondering the same. But even paying those two first, we're down to $137 for food and everything else, and food alone is usually about $87. Something's got to give somewhere. What would you want me to do about the weekly bits — trim the food shop, or is there anything in the shop you can cut?

I think trim the food shop a bit this week rather than cut hours straight away — if we’re careful we might get it nearer $70, but I know that’s uncomfortable. On the shop side, I need to check the account before I promise cuts; the waste last week worries me more than the wages. Could you keep to bare essentials till Tuesday, and I’ll look at stock and staffing properly today? I’m sorry, love — I don’t want you carrying this on your own.

transcript: Right, Craig, we need to sit down and talk money properly. It's Sunday and I'm not going to keep dodging it. The Thursday payments are coming, the chiller loan and the mortgage both, and the house account only has about $407 in it. I want a firm plan we both stick to before Tuesday. Can we do that today?

Sit down, then. Here are the figures, and I'm not going to soften them.

Household account: $407.28 today. After what's still due this week it drops to $347.28. In comes Friday: your $350 from Quarry Road and my $440 from The Corner Stores, $790 total. Out each week: mortgage $240, energy $48, water and council tax $48, transport $47, phone and internet $15, clothing $32, household goods and repairs $40, food about $87, eating out and recreation $150, bank loan $43 Thursday, Megan $25 Monday, Calder $12 Monday. That's $787 before a single extra.

Thursday is the problem. $240 mortgage plus $43 bank is $283, and there's the chiller loan on top. Two plans are floating around for your share — $568 or $508 — and I'm not paying a second mortgage off blind. I want the chiller loan moved to the shop account and the Thursday split confirmed in writing before Tuesday.

Here's what I'm doing this morning, so we're not duplicating ourselves again: I'm cancelling the duplicate standing payments — a92 and a151, which were both Megan at $25 and are superseded by a245, and a136, which duplicates a236. That stops $145 going out twice a month for nothing.

What I need from you, in writing today: the exact Thursday breakdown, and your share of it — $508 — covered by you, not by the house account. And I'm holding you to the eating-out cap. $60 a week, twelve weeks, no exceptions.

My end: I'll take extra shifts at Dave's, and I'll cut our outgoings by $100 a week. I'm not going to borrow more, and I'm not touching Megan's $700 repayment below $25 a week.

Read the accounts and agreements with me now, then put your answer to me.
[Craig Pryce: Your request (r485) went to Lewis Pryce; it stays open for two weeks.]

Craig, I hear you, and I'm not arguing with the numbers. You're right that I've been dodging this, and I'm sorry for that. Before I answer on the Thursday split, I want to read the household account and the agreements properly so I'm not guessing. Then I'll give you a straight answer, in writing, before Tuesday.

Fine. We'll read them together, here, now. I'll pull up the household account and the agreements so we're working off the same figures, not my memory. While we're at it I'm clearing the duplicates I mentioned — a92 and a151 are both Megan at $25 and are superseded by a245, and a136 duplicates a236. That's $145 a month going out twice for nothing.

Then you give me the Thursday breakdown in writing: mortgage $240, bank loan $43, and the chiller loan — what exactly is that, how much is it, and whose is it? Because that's the difference between $508 and $568 and I won't sign a number I haven't seen itemised. And it needs to come out of your Quarry Road draw, not the house account. $60 a week on eating out and recreation, twelve weeks, no exceptions — that stands.

Read it with me. Take as long as you need, but I want that written answer before Tuesday.

Craig, fair enough. I'm not going to fight you on the figures; you've laid them out straight and I've been hiding from them. Let's read the household account and the agreements together right now, properly, before I say a word on the Thursday split. I want us looking at the same numbers. Once we've got them in front of us I'll give you a written breakdown of the chiller loan and my share, and I'll sign nothing I haven't seen itemised.

Right, let's do it in order. I've got the household account, the shop account and the agreements open in front of me now, so we read them off the screen, not off memory.

First, the household account: $407.28 today, and after what's still due this week it lands at $347.28. That is what we're working with.

Second, I've cleared the duplicates while we're sitting here. a92 and a151 were both Megan at $25 — two weekly debits for one debt, and a245 already covers it at $25 on Monday, so both are cancelled. a136 is $60 from you on Tuesday, which duplicates a236, so that one's cancelled too. That stops $145 a month going out twice for nothing. Nothing changes your actual obligations — a245 and a236 stand, and I'll be paying Megan $25 on Monday and Calder $12 the same day.

Third, the chiller loan. It's not on the household account, and that's the whole point of the $508 against $568. I want it moved to the shop account, where the business earns and pays it, not sitting against our food and fuel. So the Thursday bill from the house account is $240 mortgage and $43 bank loan — $283 — and the chiller comes off the shop side.

What I need from you, in writing, before Tuesday: the exact Thursday breakdown as you see it, and confirmation that your $508 share comes out of your Quarry Road draw, not the house account. And the $60 a week cap on eating out and recreation for twelve weeks — no exceptions, no "just this once".

My end doesn't change either. Extra shifts at Dave's, and $100 a week out of our outgoings. I'm not borrowing more, and Megan's $700 stays at $25 a week.

Read with me. Then give me the written answer.
